fetched_contents.text: Estimation of Number of Graphene Layers Using Different Methods: A Focused Review Abstract Graphene, a two-dimensional nanosheet, is composed of carbon species (sp2 hybridized carbon atoms) and is the center of attention for researchers due to its extraordinary physicochemical (e.g., optical transparency, electrical, thermal conductivity, and mechanical) properties. Graphene can be synthesized using top-down or bottom-up approaches and is used in the electronics and medical (e.g., drug delivery, tissue engineering, biosensors) fields as well as in photovoltaic systems. However, the mass production of graphene and the means of transferring monolayer graphene for commercial purposes are still under investigation. When graphene layers are stacked as flakes, they have substantial impacts on the properties of graphene-based materials, and the layering of graphene obtained using different approaches varies. The determination of number of graphene layers is very important since the properties exhibited by monolayer graphene decrease as the number of graphene layer per flake increases to 5 as few-layer graphene, 10 as multilayer graphene, and more than 10 layers, when it behaves like bulk graphite. Thus, this review summarizes graphene developments and production. In addition, the efficacies of determining the number of graphene layers using various characterization methods (e.g., transmission electron microscopy (TEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), Raman spectra and mapping, and spin hall effect-based methods) are compared. Among these methods, TEM and Raman spectra were found to be most promising to determine number of graphene layers and their stacking order. Keywords: graphene, properties, sp2 hybridized carbon atoms, synthesis, applications 1. Introduction The 6th element of the periodic table is truly fascinating [1]. From the perspective of graphene chemistry, carbon has several allotropes and, when combined with various organic and inorganic molecules, can form an almost infinite number of hybrids. For example, it can be used to produce a soft lubricating material, such as graphite, and at the other end of the scale it can form diamond, the hardest material known. The most famous allotropes of carbon are 0-dimensional (0D) fullerenes [2], 1D carbon nanotubes [3], and 2D graphene [4]. Graphene is perhaps the most interesting carbon allotrope from the viewpoint of research and potential applications due to its fascinating properties [4,5]. Graphene can be categorized based on the number of graphene layers (L), stacked as monolayer graphene (1 L), few-layer graphene (<5 L), multilayer graphene (<10 L), or graphene nanoplatelets (>10 L) [6]. Around 70 years ago, scientists debated whether two-dimensional (2D) materials existed due to their thermodynamical instability [7,8]. Graphene (or “2D graphite”) was considered for 60 years [9,10,11] and was used to describe the properties of various carbon-based materials. Forty years later, it was understood that graphene provides a good condensed-matter analog of (2 + 1)-dimensional quantum electrodynamics [12,13,14], and, in 2004, it was synthesized by exfoliation of HOPG using adhesive tape. This innovation has since fueled a great number of investigations aimed at understanding the unique electronic structure of graphene. Ganguly et al. described that colloidal graphene is a key component for the molecular dispersion of graphene sheets [15]. Graphite has a 3D structure with large particle sizes and a small surface area, whereas graphene is monoatomic in thickness and has small particle sizes and an extremely high surface area; these characteristics have remarkable effects on its properties [4,5]. Accordingly, extensive research has been conducted to produce graphene in bulk for various applications, especially for electronics and batteries. Several studies have been performed to produce graphene flakes with different numbers of layers. Today graphene can be synthesized using top-down [5,16,17,18,19,20,21] or bottom-up approaches [15,22,23,24,25,26]. Top-down approaches include scotch tape exfoliation [5], liquid-phase exfoliation in different solvents [18], or chemical synthesis using redox reactions [19,20,21], whereas bottom-up approaches include chemical vapor deposition (CVD) [22,23,24] and molecular beam epitaxy [25,26]. Regardless of the method used, the number of graphene layers per flake, importantly, determines the properties of the produced materials. Before we describe earlier work on graphene, one needs to understand what a 2D crystal is. Atoms arranged regularly in a single plane form a 2D crystal, and 100 layers of such planes would be considered a thin 3D film, which prompts the question of “how many layers are needed to make a 3D structure?” It has been shown that electronic structures rapidly evolve with the number of layers and graphite approaches the 3D limit at 10 layers [27]. In this review, we focus on the techniques that are commonly used to determine the number of graphene layers. Obraztsova et al. provided a statistical analysis of AFM and Raman spectra for the determination of the number of graphene layers in graphene flake [28]. Ganguly et al. further characterized nanoparticles decorated with reduced graphene oxide and TEM investigations showed that the distinct nanoparticles were in range of 12–35 nm over reduced graphene oxide [29]. Plachá et al. reviewed graphene-based materials for various applications, such as biomedical applications [30]. Kamedulski et al. described an effective method for obtaining N-doped graphene using gamma radiation [31]. Yu et al. demonstrate the role of oxygen containing functional groups in performing water purification for graphene-oxide-based membranes [32]. 2. In the case of graphene, it is often used in combination with other techniques, such as Raman and AFM, because XRD is most effective for thicker or more crystalline samples rather than ultra-thin monolayer graphene [N4-R2].

### Which graphene-related phases or structures XRD can identify
XRD can identify several graphene-related phases and structures. It is commonly used to detect graphene oxide (GO) and reduced graphene oxide (rGO), where the XRD pattern can reveal oxidation, reduction, and structural changes [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R1]. For GO, a sharp and intense peak at around 2θ ≈ 11° is typical, which corresponds to the interlayer spacing associated with the oxidized structure [N6-R1]. In rGO, the peak broadening and shift compared to graphite indicate reduced oxidization and the recovery of graphite-like stacking [N6-R4]. XRD is also used to detect graphene itself, but its role is more indirect and supportive than definitive for single layers [N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that XRD is used to confirm the crystallinity and structural purity of graphene and related materials, including graphite, GO, and rGO samples [N2-F2][N5-R5].

### How diffraction peaks from graphene layers are interpreted
Diffraction peaks from graphene layers are interpreted through peak position, intensity, and broadening. For graphite, the strongest peak is typically at around 26.6°, corresponding to the (002) reflection and the interlayer spacing of graphite [N6-R4]. In GO, the peak is less intense and may appear at around 11°, indicating a different interlayer structure [N5-R1][N6-R1]. In rGO, the peak broadens and shifts compared to graphite, reflecting the partial restoration of graphite-like stacking and reduced interlayer disorder [N5-R4][N6-R4]. The literature also suggests that Scherrer’s equation can be used to estimate crystallite size from the (001) reflection peak in GO, with peak broadening linked to layer thickness and disorder [N2-R3]. In the context of graphene, the in-plane XRD study shows that monolayer and few-layer 2D materials can produce weak or absent peaks under conventional Bragg-Brentano geometry, indicating that peak interpretation depends strongly on sample geometry and crystallinity [N3-F3].

### What experimental conditions improve XRD detection of graphene
Several experimental conditions can improve XRD detection of graphene and related materials. First, sample preparation is critical: the evidence notes that weak diffraction and peak broadening are common for thin films and low-density materials, suggesting that poor crystallinity or amorphous content can degrade detection [N3-F3][N3-R4]. ### Which graphene-related phases or structures XRD can identify
XRD can identify several graphene-related phases and structures. It is commonly used to detect graphene oxide (GO) and reduced graphene oxide (rGO), where the XRD pattern can reveal oxidation, reduction, and structural changes [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R1]. For GO, a sharp and intense peak at around 2θ ≈ 11° is typical, which corresponds to the interlayer spacing associated with the oxidized structure [N6-R1]. In rGO, the peak broadening and shift compared to graphite indicate reduced oxidization and the recovery of graphite-like stacking [N6-R4]. XRD is also used to detect graphene itself, but its role is more indirect and supportive than definitive for single layers [N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that XRD is used to confirm the crystallinity and structural purity of graphene and related materials, including graphite, GO, and rGO samples [N2-F2][N5-R5].

Diffraction peaks from graphene layers are interpreted through peak position, intensity, and broadening. For graphite, the strongest peak is typically at around 26.6°, corresponding to the (002) reflection and the interlayer spacing of graphite [N6-R4]. In GO, the peak is less intense and may appear at around 11°, indicating a different interlayer structure [N5-R1][N6-R1]. In rGO, the peak broadens and shifts compared to graphite, reflecting the partial restoration of graphite-like stacking and reduced interlayer disorder [N5-R4][N6-R4]. The literature also suggests that Scherrer’s equation can be used to estimate crystallite size from the (001) reflection peak in GO, with peak broadening linked to layer thickness and disorder [N2-R3]. In the context of graphene, the in-plane XRD study shows that monolayer and few-layer 2D materials can produce weak or absent peaks under conventional Bragg-Brentano geometry, indicating that peak interpretation depends strongly on sample geometry and crystallinity [N3-F3].

Several experimental conditions can improve XRD detection of graphene and related materials. First, sample preparation is critical: the evidence notes that weak diffraction and peak broadening are common for thin films and low-density materials, suggesting that poor crystallinity or amorphous content can degrade detection [N3-F3][N3-R4]. Third, the use of appropriate sample mounting and alignment can reduce background noise and improve peak visibility [N5-R2][N6-R2]. Finally, the literature suggests that combining XRD with other techniques such as Raman or AFM is often useful because XRD alone is not sufficient for resolving single-layer graphene [N4-R2][N2-F2].

Overall, XRD is most useful for identifying graphene-related phases, detecting structural changes in GO and rGO, and supporting layer-count estimates when combined with other methods. XRD is most useful in three main situations: (1) when the material is not monolayer graphene and has a detectable crystalline structure, (2) when the objective is to confirm the reduction of GO to graphene or the structural recovery of rGO, and (3) when rapid, non-destructive phase analysis is needed [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4]. Similarly, TEM is highlighted as a more direct method for layer counting and structural analysis [N2-F2].

Conflicting XRD results should be interpreted cautiously, because XRD alone cannot fully resolve single-layer graphene or layer-counting details. The evidence shows that XRD results can be weak, broad, or absent for ultra-thin materials, making them difficult to interpret by themselves [N3-F3][N3-R4]. Conflicting results are therefore a sign to cross-check with complementary data rather than accept XRD as the sole evidence [N2-F2][N4-R2].

### Practical guidance for choosing XRD over alternative techniques
Practical guidance for choosing XRD over alternative techniques depends on the sample and the question being asked. XRD should be chosen when the priority is rapid, non-destructive phase identification, when the sample is thicker or more crystalline, or when the goal is to confirm the reduction state of GO or rGO [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4]. It is also useful when the question is about crystallinity, interlayer spacing, or structural disorder, especially when combined with peak broadening analysis [N2-R3][N5-R3][N5-R4]. If the sample is expected to be ultra-thin or if the signal is weak, the workflow should prioritize XRD only after verifying with more sensitive layer-counting methods [N3-F3][N4-R2].

## How is X-ray Diffraction (XRD) used to characterize graphene materials?

XRD is used primarily as a **structural analytical tool** for graphene-related materials rather than as a direct layer-counting technique for single graphene layers. Its main role is to identify **crystalline phases, structural changes, and phase purity** in graphene-related samples [N1-R3][N2-F2]. The evidence shows that XRD is especially useful for confirming the **reduction of graphene oxide (GO) to graphene** and for identifying structural changes in **graphite, GO, and reduced graphene oxide (rGO)** [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R1][N6-R4]. In practice, it is often combined with other techniques such as **Raman spectroscopy, AFM, and TEM** because XRD alone is not sufficient for resolving single-layer graphene [N4-R2][N2-F2].

### Which graphene-related phases or structures XRD can identify

XRD can identify several key graphene-related phases and structures:
- **Graphene oxide (GO)**: XRD is used to detect oxidation, and GO typically shows a sharp and intense peak around **2θ ≈ 11°**, corresponding to the oxidized interlayer structure [N6-R1][N5-R1].
- **Reduced graphene oxide (rGO)**: XRD is used to detect reduction and structural recovery. rGO shows peak broadening and shifts compared to graphite, indicating partial restoration of graphite-like stacking and reduced interlayer disorder [N6-R4][N5-R4].
- **Graphite**: The strongest graphite peak is typically around **26.6°**, corresponding to the (002) reflection and the interlayer spacing of graphite [N6-R4].
- **Multilayer graphene**: XRD can detect thicker, more crystalline graphene samples where diffraction peaks are visible and interpretable [N3-F3][N6-R4].
- **Graphene-related phase changes**: XRD is used to confirm phase changes and structural transitions in graphene materials [N1-R3].

### How diffraction peaks from graphene layers are interpreted

Diffraction peaks from graphene layers are interpreted by **peak position, intensity, broadening, and overlap with other phases**. In graphite, the strongest peak at around **26.6°** reflects the (002) interlayer spacing [N6-R4]. In GO, the peak is less intense and may appear at around **11°**, indicating a different interlayer structure [N5-R1][N6-R1]. In rGO, the peak broadens and shifts relative to graphite, reflecting the partial recovery of graphite-like stacking and reduced disorder [N6-R4][N5-R4]. The evidence also notes that **Scherrer’s equation** can be used to estimate crystallite size from the (001) reflection peak in GO, with peak broadening linked to layer thickness and disorder [N2-R3]. In ultra-thin or low-density materials, conventional Bragg-Brentano geometry struggles to detect meaningful diffraction features, and the peak signal can be weak or absent [N3-F3].

### What experimental conditions improve XRD detection of graphene

Several experimental conditions improve XRD detection of graphene and related materials:
- **Sample preparation**: Weak diffraction and peak broadening are common for thin films and low-density materials, so poor crystallinity or amorphous content can degrade detection [N3-R4][N3-F3].
- **Diffraction geometry**: In-plane XRD was specifically developed to better analyze 2D films because conventional Bragg-Brentano geometry is poorly suited for ultra-thin layers [N3-F3].
- **Sample mounting and alignment**: Reducing background noise and improving peak visibility is important, especially when the sample is thin or poorly crystalline [N5-R2][N6-R2].
- **Combined use with other techniques**: XRD is most useful when used alongside Raman, AFM, and TEM because it is not sufficient on its own to resolve single-layer graphene [N4-R2][N2-F2].

## What are the limitations of XRD in detecting single graphene layers?

XRD has several important limitations when detecting **single graphene layers**. The literature states that the ultra-thin nature of 2D layers presents a challenge to XRD analysis with conventional Bragg-Brentano geometry, making crystallinity and epitaxial orientation analysis difficult [N3-F3]. In one direct example, epitaxial graphene on SiC produced **no graphene-related peaks** in in-plane XRD, even though its presence was confirmed by Raman spectroscopy [N3-F3]. This indicates that XRD is not reliable as a standalone method for confirming monolayer graphene.

### Why single-layer graphene is difficult to detect by XRD

Single-layer graphene is difficult to detect by XRD mainly because of its **extreme thinness** and **weak diffraction response**. The evidence explicitly notes that the signal of a thin layer may be too weak to be detected in the presence of stronger reflections and background [N3-R4]. For graphene, this means that even if the material is present, its diffraction peak may not be strong enough to stand out, especially if the sample contains overlapping or stronger reflections from the substrate or other phases [N3-F3][N3-R4]. The evidence also implies that single-layer graphene may not produce a detectable peak at all under standard conditions, whereas multilayer graphene or more crystalline samples can produce visible diffraction features [N3-F3].

### Peak broadening, background noise, and overlap with other phases

Peak broadening, background noise, and overlap with other phases are major limitations for XRD in graphene detection. The evidence shows that GO exhibits peak broadening around **26°**, associated with lower crystallinity and more disorder compared to graphite [N5-R3][N6-R4]. Similarly, the broader and less intense XRD pattern of GO compared to graphite indicates that disorder and layer disorder reduce peak sharpness [N5-R2][N6-R4]. Background noise is also a problem for thin films, as the signal of a thin layer can be overwhelmed by stronger reflections or by background contributions [N3-R4]. Overlap with other phases is another issue: the literature repeatedly suggests that XRD is not sufficient on its own to resolve single-layer graphene, and that the presence of substrates or other crystalline phases can obscure the graphene signal [N4-R2][N3-F3].

### Sensitivity limits and false-negative possibilities

The sensitivity limits of XRD make it possible for single-layer graphene to be missed as a **false negative**. The evidence explicitly notes that the signal of a thin layer can be too weak to be detected, implying that XRD may fail to identify single-layer graphene even when it is present [N3-R4]. The same source also states that conventional Bragg-Brentano geometry is poorly suited for analyzing ultra-thin 2D layers, suggesting that the method may not be sensitive enough to distinguish single layers from amorphous or poorly ordered material [N3-F3]. Because of these limitations, XRD is not reliable as a standalone method for confirming monolayer graphene; the literature repeatedly supports this by citing complementary techniques such as **Raman** and **AFM** as more promising for layer counting and stacking order [N4-R2][N2-F2].

## How does XRD fit into a broader characterization workflow for graphene?

XRD fits into the broader characterization workflow for graphene as a **complementary structural tool**, best used when the goal is to confirm **crystallinity, phase purity, or structural changes** rather than to resolve single-layer graphene [N1-R3][N3-F3]. It is most useful when the sample is **not monolayer graphene** and has a detectable crystalline structure [N4-R2]. It is especially useful for thicker or more crystalline samples such as GO, rGO, and graphite, where it can detect phase transitions and structural changes [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4]. In contrast, it is less useful for single-layer graphene itself, because the material is too thin and weakly diffracting under conventional XRD geometry [N3-F3][N3-R4].

### When XRD is most useful versus when other methods are better

XRD is most useful in the following situations:
- When the material is **not monolayer graphene** and has a detectable crystalline structure.
- When the objective is to **confirm the reduction of GO to graphene** or the structural recovery of rGO.
- When the goal is to provide **rapid, non-destructive phase analysis** [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4].
- When the sample is **thicker or more crystalline**, so diffraction peaks are visible and interpretable [N6-R4].

Other methods are better when the question is about **monolayer graphene, layer counting, or stacking order**. The literature explicitly states that **Raman and AFM** are more promising for determining the number of graphene layers and their stacking order, while **TEM** is a more direct method for layer counting and structural analysis [N4-R1][N4-R2][N2-F2]. Therefore, XRD should be used in parallel with these techniques when the sample is likely to be few-layer or monolayer graphene [N4-R2][N2-F2].

### How to interpret conflicting XRD results with other data

Conflicting XRD results should be interpreted cautiously, because XRD alone cannot fully resolve single-layer graphene or layer-counting details. The evidence shows that XRD results can be **weak, broad, or absent** for ultra-thin materials, making them difficult to interpret by themselves [N3-F3][N3-R4]. When XRD does not show a clear peak, this should not be interpreted as definitive absence of graphene; instead, it may reflect **low density, weak diffraction, peak broadening, or overlap with other phases** [N3-F3][N5-R3][N5-R2]. The best approach is to **combine XRD with other techniques**: for example, if XRD suggests disorder or a peak shift, Raman can confirm layer count and stacking, while AFM can provide thickness and morphology information [N2-F2][N4-R2][N4-R4]. Conflicting results are therefore a sign to cross-check with complementary data rather than accept XRD as the sole evidence [N2-F2][N4-R2].

### Practical guidance for choosing XRD over alternative techniques

Practical guidance for choosing XRD over alternative techniques depends on the sample and the question being asked. XRD should be chosen when the priority is:
- **Rapid, non-destructive phase identification**.
- **Confirmation of phase changes** such as the reduction of GO to graphene or structural recovery in rGO.
- **Analysis of crystallinity and interlayer spacing**.
- **Support for layer-count estimates**, especially when used in combination with other methods [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4][N2-R3].

However, XRD should **not** be used as the primary method for determining **monolayer graphene**, because its sensitivity for single layers is limited by thinness and weak diffraction [N3-F3][N3-R4]. In practice, XRD is best used in parallel with **Raman, AFM, and TEM**, especially when the sample is likely to be few-layer or monolayer graphene, because those methods are more directly informative for layer count and stacking [N4-R2][N2-F2][N4-R4]. If the sample is expected to be ultra-thin or if the signal is weak, the workflow should prioritize XRD only after verifying with more sensitive layer-counting methods [N3-F3][N4-R2].

## Bottom line

XRD is a powerful structural tool for graphene characterization, but its place in the workflow is best understood as **complementary rather than definitive**. It is most useful for thicker or more crystalline samples, for confirming phase changes in GO and rGO, and for supporting layer-count estimates [N1-R3][N5-R1][N6-R4][N2-F2]. It is less useful for single-layer graphene itself, where its sensitivity is limited by the ultra-thin nature of the material and weak diffraction response [N3-F3][N3-R4]. For a complete characterization, XRD should be combined with Raman, AFM, and TEM, especially when the question is whether a sample contains monolayer graphene [N4-R2][N2-F2].
